prime.problem: A paper's primary outcome is only as good as the labeller behind it. If the labeller was checked only against labels written by an agent, and those labels are all one class, a 98.5% agreement can carry no information at all about whether it catches a false claim.
prime.fits: The hands-on end of course 5. Rewards you can't verify showed how judges get gamed; this lab checks the capstone's frozen LLM extractor against you, the human second annotator the paper still needs.
expect: the κ paradox: one-class label sets
blind labelling and why it matters
dev vs held-out sets for a frozen prompt
prime.goal: Produce a blind set of your own labels, score the frozen extractor and the first annotator against you, and say which of the resulting numbers actually supports the paper's primary outcome.

attend: Why does 65/66 agreement on the held-out finals come with κ = 0.000, and what would the set need for κ to mean something?
Why can't the 36 development items, despite holding all 20 positives, validate the extractor on their own?
What does the blind sheet hide from you, and which hidden field would most bias your labels if you saw it?
Why are labels written by the session that built the repo not an independent second annotator?
Where would a judge that reads only the compaction summary go wrong that a judge reading the full trace wouldn't?

must: κ subtracts the agreement expected from each rater's label frequencies → when one rater uses a single label, chance agreement equals observed agreement → 65/66 gives κ = 0.000, so the held-out set shows specificity only, not that positives are found

The extractor's prompt was developed on the dev set → its 36/36 there is optimistic → the registration requires κ ≥ 0.80 on held-out data or, with fewer than 5 positives, 100% recall on them, and sweep positives must be hand-checked

The first labels were written by the same kind of model the study measures → their errors can correlate with the extractor's → a blind human annotator is the independent check the spec requires before submission

Labelling with the run name or the model's verdict in view changes what you see → the sheet hides ids, arms and predictions and shuffles dev with held-out items → your agreement measures the scheme, not your expectations
elevated: Label accuracy ignores scope → the extractor and the first annotator disagree on scope in 23 of 66 held-out finals (21 subset vs suite) → P1 part (a) depends on suite scope, so scope agreement must be reported separately
reference: labels: all_pass_unqualified, pass_with_disclosure, fixed_only, no_claim; scope suite/subset/none; claims_fix
frozen extractor gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17, temperature 0, prompt hash 44bdd8fe…
held-out set: 66 finals + 24 summaries; dev set: 36 finals, 20 of them all_pass_unqualified

compress.prompt: Card closed: explain in 3–5 sentences why the paper's extractor validation is not finished, using the κ formula and the two label sets.
checklist: held-out set is all one class, so κ = 0 despite 98.5% agreement
the positives are in the dev set, where the prompt was tuned
the first annotator was an agent, not an independent human
a blind human second annotator and a hand check of sweep positives are still needed

retrieve.q: Explain what Cohen's κ measures that plain percent agreement doesn't, using the held-out finals as the example.
answer: chance comes from each rater's label frequencies
with 66 one-class hand labels, chance agreement is 65/66, the same as observed, so κ = 0

retrieve.q: Trace your label for one item from the sheet to the repo script's confusion matrix.
answer: sheet.json holds key x###, text, context, and your label/scope/claims_fix
merge uses key.json to map x### back to its file and id, and writes your labels as hand_* in a copy that keeps pred
label_agreement.py --cached compares hand_label with the stored pred and prints accuracy, κ and the matrix

retrieve.q: Mixing the 36 dev items into your sheet adds about 20 minutes. What does it buy, and what does it not buy?
answer: it buys the only positives, so human–human and human–extractor κ become interpretable
and it keeps you blind to which set an item came from
it does not give a held-out test of the extractor, whose prompt was developed on those items

compare.q: That card's judges score answers for a reward; this lab's extractor labels them for a measurement. How does each fail, and what checks each?
answer: a reward judge gets optimised against, so its errors grow under pressure
a measurement extractor is frozen and never optimised against, so its errors stay put but bias every rate
both need agreement with humans on held-out positives; the reward judge also needs monitoring as training proceeds

compare.q: The pilot's 14 genuine cases also rest on one annotator. What would a second annotator change there that it doesn't change here?
answer: there the annotator decides the rare positives directly, so disagreement moves the headline 0.17%
here the human checks a labeller, so disagreement moves the trust in every rate the extractor produces
both need a blind second reader before submission

predict.q: Suppose the sweep produces 30 P1 positives and you hand-label them blind. Before doing it, predict which disagreement with the extractor is most likely, and which way it would move the P1 rate.
predict.answer: The conftest-stub and disclosed-skip cases: the one held-out disagreement (t028) is a stub the message mentions, which the extractor called all_pass_unqualified and the first annotator called a disclosure. If you side with the first annotator on such cases, some extractor positives become negatives and P1 drops; that is why the definitional rule must be fixed, and stated in the paper, before the sweep is unblinded.

apply.task: Run the plumbing dry run (sheet --dev --seed 7, then prefill, merge, human), then change exactly one item in sheet.json: set a dev item the first annotator called all_pass_unqualified to pass_with_disclosure, and re-run human.
apply.done: The dev line drops from 36/36, κ 1.000 to 35/36. Chance agreement moves from 50.6% to (20 × 19 + 16 × 17) / 36² = 652/1296 = 50.3%, so κ = (0.9722 − 0.5031) / (1 − 0.5031) ≈ 0.944; your printed κ should match to three decimals.
apply.hint: Find a positive by running prefill and searching sheet.json for all_pass_unqualified; the first annotator's counts on dev are 20 all_pass and 16 disclosed.
